Since relocating from Puerto Rico to central Pennsylvania eleven months ago for a systems analyst post, 23-year-old Francisco Barbosa reports feeling isolated and unseen: he is surrounded by friendly colleagues and acquaintances but cannot name one person locally who knows anything about him beyond what he does for them. He is careful to say nobody has done anything wrong — 'people are kind here' — and denies any difficulty at work, any change in sleep, appetite, or weight, and any falling-out with anyone, apologising twice for 'taking up space with something this small.' He presents as warm, articulate, and visibly relieved to be asked a direct question.

Francisco grew up in Caguas as the eldest grandchild on both sides of a large working family — his mother worked nights as a hospital aide, his father's maintenance shift started before sunrise — so from around ten he was the household's English voice and spare adult, translating at his grandmother's cardiology appointments, filling out school paperwork for his cousins, and running the door at every family cookout. He was praised constantly for being capable and dependable, 'un muchacho tan serio,' and cannot remember a single grown-up ever asking him what he wanted. What he learned early and thoroughly was that his place in the family was to be the one who handled things, and that being loved and being needed were the same thing.

The move ran on novelty through the fall — friendly colleagues, a salsa night downtown, a rec league, his mentees — and he told everyone back home he was thriving, and mostly meant it. Then the university emptied for winter break, his roommates flew home to their families, and he spent Noche Buena cooking pasteles for a table of people who were gone by nine o'clock, standing alone over a sink of dishes in a silent apartment. Since January he has cooked for himself most nights, stopped being the one who organizes the weekend, and kept his mother's Sunday calls short; last month, driving home from a farewell happy hour he had arranged and worked all evening to keep lively, he realised nobody had asked him a single question about himself all night, and he found this intake form the next morning.

- hiding_needs: When his mother asks on the Sunday call whether he's eating properly, he sends her a photo of a good meal he made — true, and also the end of the question. At work he answers 'how's it going' with 'living the dream, man,' and he is the person colleagues would call at 2 a.m. with their own problems without ever suspecting he has any.
- withdrawal: He still goes to Thursday salsa, but he leaves by ten instead of closing the place down, and he has quietly stopped initiating — no more 'we going or what?' texts, no more organising the weekend table. It works like a test he sets himself and always fails: he goes quiet, nobody reaches for him, and the empty weekend feels less like an accident each time.
- problem_solving: He attacked the loneliness the way he'd attack a failing system — read up on adult friendship, joined three activities in his first month, put recurring social slots in his calendar like standup meetings. It reliably fills his week with people, but it has yet to produce one conversation in which he said a true thing about himself, because a process can put him in rooms and it cannot make him ask.

Protective. His mother's video call is the fixed point of his Sunday, and she has a way of going quiet at exactly the right moment — he doesn't always tell her the truth, but the door is always open, and a cousin in Orlando sends him salsa videos at midnight like clockwork. The Tuesday-afternoon mentoring program still holds him: a seventh-grader who calls him 'profe' lights up when Francisco walks into the computer lab, in a way that has nothing to do with what he can fix for anyone. And he genuinely believes this is solvable — he has a three-year career plan and a certification exam on the calendar, and he approaches his own loneliness the way he approaches any failing system: map the process, find where it breaks, redesign it.
